'''D'Amato:''' {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} | title = U.S. Senator | before_election = [[Al D'Amato]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Chuck Schumer]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Elections in New York (state) sidebar}} The '''1998 United States Senate election in New York''' was held November 3, 1998. Republican incumbent [[Al D'Amato]] ran for a fourth term in office but was defeated by Democratic U.S. representative [[Chuck Schumer]] in the "high[est] profile and nastiest" contest of the [[1998 United States elections]].{{cite news| url=http://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/stories/1998/11/03/election/senate/new.york/ | work=CNN | title =Schumer topples D'Amato in New York Senate race|date=November 3, 1998|last1=Rothenburg|first1=Stuart}} Primary elections were held on September 15. Schumer defeated the early favorite for the Democratic nomination, television host and [[1984 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection|1984 vice presidential nominee]] [[Geraldine Ferraro]], who was making her second unsuccessful bid to face D'Amato. The third candidate in the Democratic race was [[New York City Public Advocate|New York City public advocate]] [[Mark Green (New York politician)|Mark Green]], whom D'Amato had defeated in a 1986 landslide. Schumer was also nominated by the [[Liberal Party of New York|Liberal]] and [[Independence Party of New York|Independence]] parties, while D'Amato was nominated by the [[Conservative Party of New York State|Conservative]] and [[New York State Right to Life Party|Right to Life]] parties. This was the first time since [[1950 United States Senate election in New York|1950]] that Democrats won the Class 3 United States Senate seat from New York, and the last time an incumbent U.S. Senator from New York lost a general election. Schumer's swearing in marked the first time since 1947 that Democrats held both of New York's U.S. Senate seats. == Democratic primary == === Candidates === * [[Geraldine Ferraro]], host of ''[[Crossfire (American TV program)|Crossfire]]'', former U.S. representative from [[Queens]], [[1984 United States presidential election|1984]] nominee for [[Vice President of the United States|vice president]], and 1992 candidate for U.S. Senate * [[Mark Green (New York politician)|Mark Green]], [[New York City Public Advocate|New York City public advocate]] and [[United States Senate election in New York, 1986|1986]] nominee for U.S. Senate (''also running as Independence'') * Eric Ruano-Melendez, perennial candidate{{citation needed|date=October 2022}} * [[Chuck Schumer]], U.S. representative from [[Brooklyn]] (''also running as Liberal and Independence'') === Campaign === Ferraro was well known for having been the [[1984 United States presidential election|1984 Democratic vice presidential nominee]], and had also run, but lost, in the Democratic primary in the [[United States Senate election in New York, 1992|1992 U.S. Senate election in New York]]. Green had been the Democratic nominee in the [[United States Senate election in New York, 1986|1986 election]], but lost in the general election to D'Amato. At the start of 1998, Ferraro had done no fund-raising, out of fear of conflict of interest with her job, hosting the [[CNN]] program ''[[Crossfire (U.S. TV program)|Crossfire]]'', but was nonetheless perceived as the front-runner by virtue of her name recognition;{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/01/04/nyregion/friends-say-ferraro-will-seek-d-amato-s-seat.html | title = Friends Say Ferraro Will Seek D'Amato's Seat | author = Nagourney, Adam | author-link = Adam Nagourney | work = [[The New York Times]] | date=January 4, 1998}} indeed, December and January polls had her 25 percentage points ahead of Green in the race, and even further ahead of Schumer.{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/09/17/nyregion/the-1998-campaign-the-farewell-for-ferraro-early-promise-lopsided-loss.html | title =The Farewell: For Ferraro, Early Promise, Lopsided Loss | author=Waldman, Amy | work = [[The New York Times]] | date=September 17, 1998}}{{cite book | last=Schumer | first=Chuck | author-link=Chuck Schumer | title=Positively American: Winning Back the Middle-Class Majority One Family at a Time | publisher=[[Rodale Books]] | year=2007 | isbn=978-1-59486-572-5 | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/positivelyameric00schu }} p. 17. Unlike her previous campaigns, Ferraro's family finances never became an issue in 1998. However, she lost ground during the summer, with Schumer catching her in the polls by early August, and then soon passing her.Schumer, ''Positively American'', p. 31. Schumer, a tireless fund-raiser, outspent her by a five-to-one margin, and Ferraro failed to establish a political image current with the times.Schumer, ''Positively American'', pp. 18, 30. In the September 15, 1998, primary, she was beaten soundly by Schumer, with a 51 percent to 26 percent margin. Unlike the bitter 1992 Democratic senatorial primary, this contest was not divisive, and Ferraro and third-place finisher Green endorsed Schumer at a unity breakfast the following day.Schumer, ''Positively American'', pp. 33, 39. === Polling === {| class="wikitable" |- ! When D'Amato's first strategy failed, D'Amato attacked his opponent's attendance record as a member of Congress, which Schumer refuted.{{Cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/election98/nyu_11-4.html |title=Online NewsHour: 98 Election - The New York Wrap-up - November 4, 1998 |access-date=September 17, 2017 |archive-date=January 8, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140108030430/http://www.pbs.org/newshour/election98/nyu_11-4.html |url-status=dead }}{{Cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/election98/damato_schumer/nysenate_10-28.html |title=Online NewsHour: New York Senate Race - October 28, 1998 |access-date=September 17, 2017 |archive-date=July 25, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130725215919/http://www.pbs.org/newshour/election98/damato_schumer/nysenate_10-28.html |url-status=dead }} Late in the campaign, D'Amato called Schumer a "putzhead" in a private meeting with Jewish supporters ("putz" is [[Yiddish]] for [[penis]], and can be slang for "fool"). He later apologized for the comment. In the last days of the campaign, D'Amato campaigned with popular [[Governor of New York|New York governor]] [[George Pataki]], who was also running for reelection, and was also supported by [[Mayor of New York City|New York City mayor]] [[Rudy Giuliani]] and former Democratic mayor [[Ed Koch]].{{cite news| url=http://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/stories/1998/10/30/ny.senate/ | work=CNN |last1=Randall|first1=Gene|date=October 30, 1998| title =New York Senate race an old-fashioned street fight}} [[Vice President of the United States|Vice President]] [[Al Gore]] and [[First Lady of the United States|First Lady]] [[Hillary Clinton]] personally campaigned for Schumer, as D'Amato was a prominent critic of [[President of the United States|President]] [[Bill Clinton]] who led the investigation into [[Whitewater controversy|Whitewater]]. Though the Republican Party was well organized, the Democratic Party benefited from [[robocalls]] from President Clinton and mobilization from two major unions, the [[United Federation of Teachers]] and [[1199SEIU United Healthcare Workers East|1199SEIU]]. Though D'Amato was effective in obtaining federal government funds for New York state projects during his Senate career, he failed to capitalize on this in the election. Also, Schumer was a tenacious fundraiser, and was aggressive in his attacks.{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/11/04/nyregion/1998-elections-new-york-state-senate-schumer-uses-d-amato-s-tactics-win-senate.html | work = [[The New York Times]] | title =THE 1998 ELECTIONS: NEW YORK STATE - THE SENATE; Schumer Uses D'Amato's Tactics To Win Senate Election Handily | first=Adam | last=Nagourney | date=November 4, 1998}} The candidates spent $30 million during the race. === Polling === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |- ! scope="col" style="width:300px;" | Poll source ! scope="col" style="width:130px;" | Date(s) ! scope="col" style="width:75px;" | Sample

Schumer (L) |- | Quinnipiac | June 18, 1998 | {{party shading/Republican}} | '''44%''' | 28% | 14% |} {{hidden end}} === Results === The race was ultimately not close, with Schumer defeating the incumbent D'Amato by just over 10%.{{cite web |url=http://www.elections.ny.gov/NYSBOE/elections/1998/USSENWEB.pdf |title=1998 General Election Results |website=Elections.NY.gov |access-date=July 24, 2012 |archive-date=August 23, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120823020655/http://www.elections.ny.gov/NYSBOE/elections/1998/USSENWEB.pdf |url-status=dead }} D'Amato did win a majority of New York's counties, but his wins were in less populated areas. Schumer's win is attributed to strong performance in [[New York City]]. Schumer also performed well in heavily populated upstate cities, like [[Buffalo, New York|Buffalo]], [[Syracuse, New York|Syracuse]], [[Rochester, New York|Rochester]], and [[Albany, New York|Albany]].
